title: Incidence versus prevalence
dek: Prevalence is a stock. Incidence is a flow. Risk, rate, and odds are not synonyms, and duration ties the stock to the flow.
story: Prevalence P = proportion with disease at a time (or in a defined window). Incidence is new events: either a risk (proportion of a closed cohort that develops disease over time t) or a rate (events per person-time). A survey of who has TB today estimates prevalence. A cohort of household contacts estimates incidence (with incomplete follow-up, as a rate).

In a steady state, prevalence ≈ incidence rate × mean duration. Long-duration treated TB and long latency make prevalence a poor proxy for current transmission. A district can have high prevalence from old cases and falling incidence, or the reverse during an outbreak of rapid disease.

Poisson log-linear models with an offset log(person-time) target rates. Logistic models of “ever diseased in the window” target risks (or prevalences in a cross-section). Using a logit on counts without exposure time rediscovers population size (Poisson plate).
deep: Risk in a closed cohort: Yᵢ ~ Bernoulli(π), π = 1 − S(t) for a survival function. Censoring makes the Bernoulli likelihood wrong; use a hazard model or a Poisson approximation with person-time if hazards are small.
Rate: events / person-time. Two events in one person still count two in a rate (if you allow repeated events); a first-event risk would not. Define the event.

Odds = π/(1−π). Case-control studies estimate odds ratios; with rare incidence, OR ≈ rate ratio or risk ratio. TB disease in a high-burden clinic is not always rare — do not paste the rare-disease slogan onto smear-positivity.

Sampling: a prevalent case series oversamples long-duration disease (length-biased sampling). Associations with slow chronic forms will look stronger than in an incident series. For TB, that matters if you study delayed diagnosis using a cross-section of current patients.

visual.caption: Stock versus flow: incidence feeds the prevalent pool; duration (and cure/death/migration) empties it. A survey snapshots the pool. A cohort counts the arrows in. Mixing the snapshot with a Poisson rate without person-time is the usual spreadsheet error.

example.title: Same 40 cases, two captions
example.setup: District A: 40 TB diagnoses this year, 100,000 people, mean duration in the prevalent pool ~ 0.5 years (faster care). District B: 40 diagnoses, same population, mean duration ~ 2 years (slow care).

steps.title: Rates
steps.body: If 40 are incident counts, incidence looks similar (40/100,000 per year) — until you ask completeness of diagnosis.

steps.title: Prevalence cartoon
steps.body: P ≈ λ × duration. B’s snapshot survey would find about four times as many current cases if the cartoon held. High prevalence here is duration, not a four-fold outbreak.

steps.title: Model choice
steps.body: A prevalence survey wants a survey-weighted Bernoulli/logit of current disease. A notification Poisson wants person-years and a completeness story. Do not fit one and caption the other.

example.takeaway: Name stock or flow. Duration is the missing multiplier, not a footnote.

check.prompt: A household contact study that counts new TB over 18 months is targeting:

check.why: New events over time. Baseline X-ray prevalence would be a stock.
